summary:
This project is a game-based software application designed to serve as a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. Developed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, it targets a beginner/youth and intermediate audience to bridge the gap in space-themed STEM education.  
The game challenges students to run a lunar or Martian outpost, moving beyond oversimplified concepts to introduce real-world engineering trade-offs. Players must actively balance critical, competing demands—such as life support, radiation shielding, power generation, and food production—making tangible decisions that directly impact the success or failure of their mission. This interactive approach aims to make complex mission planning both accessible and engaging for young learners.
details:
Astronomous is an interactive, web-based resource management game that puts middle and high school students in the commander's seat of a Lunar or Martian outpost. Players interface with a futuristic, clean dashboard where they monitor real-time metrics for life support, power generation, food supply, and radiation shielding. As the game progresses, players are hit with dynamic events (like dust storms or solar flares) and must make immediate engineering trade-offs—such as diverting power from hydroponics to reinforce radiation shields. The game engine calculates the outcome of these choices, providing instant feedback on whether the outpost thrives or fails.

The primary benefit of Astronomous is that it makes highly complex STEM concepts tangible and experiential. Space engineering is often taught either through oversimplified sci-fi tropes or through academic material that is too dense for young learners. This game bridges that gap. By forcing players to actively juggle competing demands, they naturally learn the harsh realities of off-world survival—like the fact that thick radiation shielding increases launch weight, or that solar panels are useless during a 14-day lunar night.

The intended impact is to inspire the "Artemis generation" of future engineers, scientists, and astronauts. By transforming dry trade-off analysis into an engaging survival challenge, we aim to spark a genuine interest in space exploration and systems engineering. We want students to walk away understanding that space travel isn't just about rockets; it's about the delicate, vital balance of sustaining human life in a hostile environment.

Astronomous is creative because it subverts the typical "space game" genre. Instead of focusing on combat, flying, or abstract empire-building, it gamifies the rigorous constraints of real-world physics and engineering. It takes the very real, often tedious spreadsheets that NASA engineers use to plan missions and translates them into an addictive, fast-paced survival loop. The visual design is also creatively tailored to feel like a sleek, modern Mission Control interface rather than a toy.

The "Fun vs. Science" Balance: We heavily considered how to keep the game scientifically grounded without making it so punishingly realistic that kids would give up. We simplified complex math into intuitive resource bars (Power, Water, Food, Shielding).
Cognitive Load: We designed the UI to be clean and focused. We knew that if we flooded the screen with too many numbers and graphs, our target beginner/youth audience would get overwhelmed.
Accessibility: We prioritized making it a browser-based application so that any student with internet access could play it instantly, without needing powerful gaming hardware or heavy downloads.
